items.prompt: A legacy application writes to local disk, depends on a fixed hostname, and assumes a long-lived process. The team wants to containerize it without changing behavior first. What should happen before selecting a platform?
constraints: The first migration step should preserve known behavior.
The application has hidden host assumptions.
The team needs to identify blockers before production placement.

options.text: Inventory process, filesystem, network, hostname, privilege, licensing, startup, shutdown, and data dependencies, then classify which assumptions must be externalized or preserved.
Build an image immediately and treat any runtime error as proof that the container platform is unsuitable.
Move the application to a public subnet because containerization removes the need to understand its dependencies.
Replace every local file with an S3 object without checking access patterns, locking, or consistency requirements.

feedback.Reason: Container migration starts with dependency and operating-model discovery; packaging an application does not remove host assumptions automatically.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A container image packages user space, but runtime behavior still depends on process lifecycle, filesystems, networking, identity, privileged operations, and external services.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team records dependencies, chooses a compatible capacity model, and creates explicit remediation work for state, configuration, and host integration.
Details.errorCorrection: Immediate packaging hides risks, public networking does not solve dependency discovery, and object storage cannot replace every filesystem use case.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A faithful first move may preserve some legacy characteristics, but each retained host dependency must have an owner and a tested lifecycle.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A failed first image may reflect an undiscovered dependency rather than an unsuitable platform.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Network exposure does not replace application and host dependency analysis.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Object storage has different consistency, locking, and access semantics from a local filesystem.

items.prompt: A team packages a web server in a container, but the image starts a shell that launches the server as a background child and never forwards termination signals. Which correction improves orchestration behavior?
constraints: The orchestrator must know when the application is ready and stopped.
Graceful shutdown matters during replacement.
The container should have one clear workload process boundary.

options.text: Run the application with an explicit entrypoint or command, keep the main process in the foreground, handle termination signals, and define health checks separately.
Keep the shell as a background supervisor because orchestrators infer child health from the parent process automatically.
Increase container memory because signal handling is determined by memory size.
Use a public IP because graceful shutdown requires external clients to terminate the process.

feedback.Reason: Container schedulers manage the main process lifecycle; signal handling and foreground execution are required for reliable start, stop, and replacement.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The container entrypoint and command define the process seen by the runtime. A foreground process can receive termination signals and allow the orchestrator to observe exit status and drain traffic.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team uses an immutable entrypoint, graceful shutdown timeout, and readiness check before allowing traffic.
Details.errorCorrection: A parent shell does not automatically expose child health, memory does not define signals, and public addressing is unrelated to process lifecycle.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A supervisor can be valid when the workload truly manages multiple processes, but it must preserve signal, exit, logging, and health semantics deliberately.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: The orchestrator observes the container's main process and does not infer all child health or signal behavior.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Memory sizing does not determine signal forwarding or process foreground behavior.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Network reachability does not control graceful process shutdown.

items.prompt: The same container image must run in development, staging, and production with different endpoints and credentials. Which pattern preserves one deployable artifact?
constraints: Environment values differ by stage.
Secrets must not be baked into the image.
The image should be immutable and promoted between environments.

options.text: Keep environment-specific configuration and secrets outside the image, inject them through the deployment or runtime configuration, and grant only the workload's required access.
Build a separate image for every environment so configuration is always compiled into the artifact.
Put production credentials in the image because private registry access makes them inaccessible to the runtime.
Use a route table as the configuration registry because route entries vary by environment.

feedback.Reason: External configuration supports immutable promotion while keeping secrets and environment values outside the image artifact.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Task definitions, environment sources, parameter stores, or secret stores can provide runtime configuration. IAM and deployment ownership determine which workload can read each value.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team promotes one image digest, injects stage-specific endpoints, retrieves secrets through a managed store, and verifies that logs do not expose them.
Details.errorCorrection: Per-environment images create drift, registry privacy does not prevent the running task from exposing embedded secrets, and route tables are not configuration stores.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Runtime configuration adds deployment dependencies and change coordination; secret rotation and restart behavior must be tested.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Separate images create artifact drift and make promotion and rollback less trustworthy.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A running task or anyone with image access can retrieve embedded credentials; registry privacy is not secret management.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Route tables describe network forwarding and do not hold application configuration.

items.prompt: After migration, an application writes only to a file inside the container and operators cannot see logs after task replacement. What should change?
constraints: Tasks are replaceable.
Logs are needed for troubleshooting and audit.
The application can be configured to write structured output.

options.text: Emit structured logs to stdout or stderr where the container platform can collect them, route them to a durable sink, and define retention and sensitive-data controls.
Keep the file inside the container because the orchestrator preserves every task filesystem after replacement.
Write logs to a route table so every task can inspect the same entries.
Disable logs after migration because health checks provide all diagnostic information.

feedback.Reason: Replaceable containers need an external log collection path; task-local files are not an operational history.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Container runtimes and ECS/EKS integrations can collect stdout and stderr to logging services. A durable sink preserves records beyond task lifetime and supports centralized search and retention.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team emits JSON with request and revision identifiers, routes logs to CloudWatch or another approved sink, and redacts secrets.
Details.errorCorrection: Task files can disappear, route tables do not store logs, and health checks cannot explain application failures or user behavior.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Central logging incurs ingestion and retention cost; structured fields and retention tiers should match incident and compliance needs.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Container-local files are not a durable log history after task replacement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Route tables contain forwarding rules rather than log records.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Health checks show limited availability signals and do not replace application logs.

items.prompt: A containerized order service writes committed orders to its local filesystem, and replacements lose them. Which migration correction is required?
constraints: Committed orders must survive task replacement.
The application can use an external persistence interface.
Multiple replicas may run concurrently.

options.text: Move durable order state to a supported database or storage service with a defined ownership, transaction, backup, and access model; keep local disk for disposable scratch only.
Increase the container's ephemeral disk and assume it becomes durable when the task is managed by ECS.
Pin the service to one task so local state remains available to every request.
Store order data in the container image so every replacement starts with the latest state.

feedback.Reason: Container replacement requires business state to live in a durable service rather than task-local storage or image layers.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: ECS and EKS manage workload placement, not the durability or transactional semantics of arbitrary local filesystems. External state allows replicas and replacements to share the business truth.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team selects RDS, DynamoDB, or another fit-for-purpose service, scopes access, tests recovery, and makes handlers idempotent.
Details.errorCorrection: More ephemeral disk does not provide durability, pinning reduces availability and still fails on task loss, and images are immutable artifacts rather than live state.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: External persistence adds latency and operational dependencies but is required for correctness and recovery.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Ephemeral task storage is still tied to task lifecycle and is not a durable order store.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: One task is a failure bottleneck and does not guarantee persistence after replacement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: An image cannot capture runtime order mutations and should not contain business state.

items.prompt: A legacy container works on a flat network but fails in ECS because it calls a database by hostname and assumes all outbound ports are open. What should the design make explicit?
constraints: The database should remain private.
Only required traffic should be allowed.
Name resolution must work from task subnets.

options.text: Map required DNS names, routes, security-group flows, ports, egress, and endpoint dependencies, then implement least-privilege VPC networking and test failure paths.
Allow all inbound and outbound traffic because containers require flat-network behavior for service discovery.
Give the database a public address so the migrated task can use the old hostname behavior from anywhere.
Use an image tag to encode security-group rules because image metadata controls VPC routing.

feedback.Reason: Container migration preserves application behavior only when network dependencies are translated into explicit VPC routing, DNS, and authorization controls.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Task ENIs, route tables, security groups, DNS, endpoints, and egress controls determine connectivity. Application hostnames must resolve to the intended private targets.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team uses private subnets, allows task-to-database traffic on the database port, configures private DNS, and verifies endpoint and egress behavior.
Details.errorCorrection: Flat unrestricted access violates least privilege, public database exposure is unnecessary, and image tags do not configure VPC networking.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Private networking requires deliberate dependency mapping and can expose missing endpoints or routes as explicit unavailable states.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Unrestricted network access increases blast radius and hides the real dependency contract.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Public database placement increases exposure and is not required for private task connectivity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Image metadata does not create routes or security-group rules.

items.prompt: A deployment references the mutable `latest` image tag, so rollback sometimes starts different bytes than the original release. Which practice fixes the release contract?
constraints: The same artifact must be deployable and rollbackable.
Image content can change after a tag is pushed.
The deployment system can record an immutable identifier.

options.text: Build and scan an immutable image, promote it by digest or immutable tag, record the digest in the task definition, and retain the prior digest for rollback.
Keep using `latest` because registries guarantee that a tag always points to the original bytes.
Rebuild from source during rollback instead of retaining the tested image artifact.
Use a security group rule to pin container bytes to a deployment revision.

feedback.Reason: Immutable image identity makes deployments reproducible and rollback deterministic.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A registry tag can be moved; an image digest identifies exact content. Task definitions or deployment records should reference the tested artifact and preserve the previous version.
Details.scenarioApplication: The pipeline scans an image, records its digest, deploys that digest, and rolls back to the last known-good digest without rebuilding.
Details.errorCorrection: Mutable tags do not guarantee bytes, rebuilding may introduce drift, and network rules cannot pin an image artifact.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Digest-based promotion requires registry retention and artifact lifecycle management so rollback content remains available.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A mutable tag can point to different content over time.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Rebuilding during rollback can change dependencies and produce a different artifact.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Security groups authorize traffic and do not identify container bytes.

items.prompt: Private ECS tasks must pull images from Amazon ECR without public internet access. Which access design should be evaluated?
constraints: Tasks run in private subnets.
The registry and image are private.
The security team wants least-privilege access and auditable pulls.

options.text: Use the task execution role for ECR pull permissions and configure the required VPC endpoints, DNS, routes, and security groups for private registry access.
Make the ECR repository public because private subnets cannot pull private images.
Grant the task AdministratorAccess because pulling an image requires every AWS action.
Store the image in a route table so the task can pull it without IAM or network configuration.

feedback.Reason: Private image pulls require both the correct execution identity and private connectivity to ECR and its supporting endpoints.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: ECS task execution permissions allow image retrieval and logs; VPC endpoints and private DNS provide a path from private subnets without requiring public egress when supported.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team scopes repository access, configures ECR API and Docker endpoints as needed, validates endpoint policies, and tests task launch with public egress disabled.
Details.errorCorrection: Public repositories weaken control, image pulls do not require administrator access, and route tables cannot store image layers.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Endpoint design adds network and policy configuration, but preserves private image distribution and reduces broad egress.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Private networking can reach private ECR through supported endpoints and does not require public images.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: The execution role should grant only the image and log actions required by the task.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Route tables forward packets and do not contain registry content or replace IAM.

items.prompt: A multi-Region service must start the same approved image in a recovery Region even when the primary Region is unavailable. Which registry pattern reduces recovery dependency?
constraints: The image artifact must be available in the recovery Region.
The digest must remain identical.
Replication should not promote unapproved tags.

options.text: Configure ECR replication for the approved repositories or images, verify replicated digests and permissions in the recovery Region, and test deployment from the local copy.
Pull the image from the primary Region during recovery because cross-Region image access never depends on the primary.
Rebuild the image in the recovery Region during the outage and assume dependency versions will be identical.
Store only the image tag in Route 53 because DNS automatically replicates registry layers.

feedback.Reason: Regional image replication removes a primary-Region registry dependency and preserves the exact artifact for recovery.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: ECR cross-Region replication copies images to another registry region. Recovery still requires permissions, network access, configuration, and a tested deployment reference.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team replicates only approved repositories, records digests, validates the target repository policy, and runs a recovery deployment from the local image.
Details.errorCorrection: Primary-region pulls fail with the primary dependency, rebuilding can drift, and DNS does not replicate image layers.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Replication adds storage and transfer cost and needs lifecycle and security policy; it does not replicate application data or secrets.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A primary-Region registry can be unavailable during the exact recovery scenario.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Rebuilding during an outage may use different dependencies and produce a different artifact.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Route 53 resolves names but does not copy or store image layers.

items.prompt: A regulated workload must remain on customer-owned on-premises servers, but the team wants to use ECS APIs and task definitions for a consistent operating model. Which option should be evaluated?
constraints: Compute location is fixed on premises.
The customer owns the underlying servers.
The workload can meet ECS Anywhere prerequisites.

options.text: Evaluate ECS Anywhere for compatible external instances, while retaining responsibility for host capacity, connectivity, patching, security, and the on-premises runtime.
Use Fargate because it can place tasks on any customer-owned server without an agent or connectivity requirement.
Use S3 to execute the container locally because object storage is location-independent compute.
Use an internet-facing load balancer as the replacement for the ECS external instance agent.

feedback.Reason: ECS Anywhere extends ECS management to registered external instances but does not transfer ownership of the customer-owned infrastructure.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: External instances run the ECS agent and required components and connect to the ECS control plane. The customer remains responsible for host lifecycle, network, security, and capacity.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team validates connectivity and registration, hardens and patches hosts, limits task roles, and defines behavior when the control-plane connection is unavailable.
Details.errorCorrection: Fargate does not run on arbitrary customer servers, S3 is not local compute, and a load balancer does not replace the agent or control connection.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: ECS Anywhere provides a consistent control model but preserves on-premises operations and can introduce connectivity and support constraints.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Fargate is AWS-managed task compute and does not place tasks on arbitrary customer-owned servers.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: S3 cannot execute a container on premises.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A load balancer routes traffic and does not register or manage an external ECS instance.

items.prompt: A factory application needs low-latency access to local equipment and must keep data processing on site, but the team wants AWS-consistent infrastructure APIs. Which placement should be evaluated?
constraints: Latency to local equipment is a hard requirement.
Data residency requires local processing.
The site can host and operate AWS Outposts capacity.

options.text: Evaluate AWS Outposts for supported container or compute services at the site, and design local capacity, service limits, connectivity, patching, and failure behavior explicitly.
Use a standard public AWS Region and assume network latency to the factory is always negligible.
Use a public IP on each container so processing is local even when compute runs in the Region.
Use CloudFront as the factory compute layer because edge caching executes arbitrary container workloads on site.

feedback.Reason: Outposts can bring supported AWS infrastructure and services closer to local workloads, but local capacity and operational boundaries remain real.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Outposts is customer-site infrastructure managed as part of AWS; supported services and capacity must be verified, and the design must account for Region connectivity and local failure.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect validates container support, sizes site capacity, protects local data, and defines how workloads behave when the Outpost or Regional connection is degraded.
Details.errorCorrection: Regional latency may violate the requirement, public IPs do not move compute, and CloudFront is an edge delivery service rather than arbitrary on-site container compute.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Outposts reduces latency and supports local processing but adds site power, capacity, hardware, networking, and operational dependencies.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A Region may not meet a hard local latency or residency requirement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Addressing does not change where compute executes.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: CloudFront caches and delivers content and does not host arbitrary factory container workloads.

items.prompt: A cloud container service must call a legacy on-premises service by a stable name, while the legacy service must call back only to an internal cloud endpoint. Which design is needed?
constraints: Connectivity uses a private hybrid link.
Both sides require controlled name resolution.
The endpoints should not be public.

options.text: Use private routing and DNS forwarding or shared resolution, explicit security rules on both sides, and stable internal service endpoints with health and timeout behavior.
Publish both services to the public internet because hybrid name resolution cannot work privately.
Put the on-premises service's hostname in the container image and assume it will resolve in every network.
Use an S3 bucket as a bidirectional service-discovery registry without network or IAM design.

feedback.Reason: Hybrid service communication needs private connectivity, DNS ownership, endpoint stability, and symmetric authorization rather than public exposure or image-baked names.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: VPN or Direct Connect provides routing, while Route 53 Resolver, on-premises DNS, or other approved mechanisms provide name resolution. Security groups, firewalls, and timeouts govern traffic.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team documents DNS forwarding zones, routes, firewall ports, and failure behavior, then tests each call direction and degraded link state.
Details.errorCorrection: Private hybrid DNS is possible, image-baked names can be environment-specific, and object storage is not a live discovery protocol.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Hybrid dependencies have latency and link failure modes; asynchronous buffering or degraded states may be safer than indefinite synchronous waits.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Private hybrid connectivity and DNS can avoid public exposure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: An image does not guarantee that a hostname resolves in every deployment network.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: S3 can store configuration but is not a health-aware bidirectional service-discovery system.

items.prompt: A licensed application is tied to a physical host identifier and cannot be moved freely between nodes. What must be resolved before using an elastic container scheduler?
constraints: The license terms are binding.
Tasks may be replaced or rescheduled.
The workload owner can negotiate or redesign the license boundary.

options.text: Validate license portability and host-affinity requirements with the vendor, then choose a supported dedicated or fixed-capacity placement and recovery process if elasticity is not permitted.
Ignore the license because containers make every physical host appear identical to the vendor.
Use Spot capacity because interruption and movement do not affect licensing.
Copy the license key into every image so any task can run without tracking host identity.

feedback.Reason: Container scheduling does not override software licensing or host-affinity terms; placement and recovery must be compatible with the license.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Schedulers can replace or move tasks across capacity. A license tied to host, socket, or instance identity may require dedicated placement, vendor approval, or a different service model.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team documents license limits, isolates approved hosts, prevents accidental rescheduling, and tests failover within the permitted boundary.
Details.errorCorrection: Containers do not erase licensing obligations, Spot increases movement risk, and copying keys into images creates security and compliance exposure.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Fixed placement may reduce elasticity and increase cost; the constraint is a real architecture input, not a metadata label.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Container abstraction does not change vendor licensing terms or physical host identity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Spot interruption can violate host-affinity and license continuity requirements.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Embedding license keys creates leakage and does not prove legal or technical portability.

items.prompt: A legacy application is difficult to rewrite, but its reporting component can run independently in a container. Which migration sequence limits risk?
constraints: The legacy application must remain available.
The reporting component has a bounded interface.
Traffic can be moved gradually.

options.text: Extract the reporting capability behind an explicit contract, run it in the new container path for a controlled cohort, compare results, and retire the old path only after rollback and reconciliation evidence.
Rewrite the entire legacy application before deploying any container so no compatibility path is needed.
Run both systems as unrestricted writers to the same tables until operators decide which result looks correct.
Move the legacy VM to a different subnet and call the reporting capability containerized.

feedback.Reason: Incremental extraction narrows the change and keeps a controlled rollback path while the new containerized capability proves itself.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A stable interface and traffic or data cutover allow old and new implementations to coexist. Ownership, reconciliation, and rollback must be explicit during the transition.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team routes selected reports to the container, verifies output and latency, and removes the legacy path only after no consumer depends on it.
Details.errorCorrection: A full rewrite expands risk, unrestricted dual writes create conflicting truth, and subnet movement is not containerization.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Coexistence costs extra operations but is safer than a big-bang migration when the legacy system has unknown dependencies.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A full rewrite increases scope and removes the opportunity to learn from controlled migration.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Unrestricted dual writes create divergence and ambiguous authority.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Network relocation does not change the workload packaging or operating model.

items.prompt: A stateful legacy service is moving to a container platform, and the cutover must preserve all writes made while the new service is being validated. Which plan is safest?
constraints: Writes continue during migration.
The source of truth must be unambiguous.
The cutover needs a measured consistency check and rollback decision.

options.text: Define one write owner, replicate or migrate data with a measured lag, quiesce or coordinate writes for cutover, verify checksums and business invariants, then switch traffic with a rollback window.
Let old and new services write independently and merge conflicts after the cutover without a data ownership rule.
Copy data once and immediately switch all traffic without checking writes that occurred during the copy.
Store the migration checkpoint in a route table because network state proves data consistency.

feedback.Reason: Stateful migration needs an explicit authority and a cutover protocol that accounts for writes during replication and validation.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Data migration can have lag, duplicate, or conflicting writes. A controlled ownership transition and business-level validation reduce the risk of silent loss or divergent state.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team tracks replication position, pauses or fences writes where required, compares records and invariants, switches the owner, and preserves a tested rollback path.
Details.errorCorrection: Unowned dual writes create conflicts, a one-time copy can miss changes, and route tables cannot prove data consistency.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A write pause may affect availability; if zero downtime is mandatory, the application needs a designed dual-write or change-capture protocol with reconciliation.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Without one authority and conflict handling, dual writes can diverge irreparably.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A snapshot copy does not include writes made after the copy without change capture or a coordinated cutover.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Network metadata cannot prove that two data stores contain equivalent business state.

items.prompt: A containerized replacement passes functional tests, but the team has no equivalent alerts, dashboards, deployment evidence, or recovery runbook from the legacy service. What is missing?
constraints: Production support must continue after migration.
Functional correctness is not the only acceptance criterion.
The service has availability and recovery objectives.

options.text: Define operational parity: health and SLO metrics, structured logs, traces or correlation, deployment and capacity signals, alerts, ownership, runbooks, and a tested recovery procedure.
Treat the migration as complete because container startup proves the service is operable.
Delete legacy dashboards immediately so operators are forced to use the new container metrics.
Use a larger task size as a substitute for alerts and recovery testing.

feedback.Reason: A migration changes the operating model as well as packaging; reliability requires evidence and response paths for the new runtime.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Container orchestration exposes task, capacity, target-health, deployment, and application signals. Operators need those signals mapped to business SLOs and a tested response.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team runs failure drills, verifies dashboards and alarms, documents ownership, and keeps the old evidence until the new path is proven.
Details.errorCorrection: Startup is not operability, deleting old evidence removes comparison, and larger resources do not replace observability or runbooks.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Operational parity may require new instrumentation and costs, but without it the migration creates an unsupported production path.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A running container does not prove that operations can detect, diagnose, or recover from failure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Removing old evidence before proving the new path increases migration risk.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Capacity size cannot replace alerts, ownership, or recovery procedures.

items.prompt: A new container revision produces incorrect invoices after 10% of traffic has migrated. Which rollback action is safest?
constraints: The previous revision is still available.
Invoice writes may have started.
The team must preserve evidence and avoid creating a second data error.

options.text: Stop or reverse traffic to the known-good revision, preserve the failed revision and correlation evidence, assess and reconcile any writes, then fix and redeploy through the tested path.
Delete the failed image and task definition immediately so no operator can accidentally inspect it.
Keep sending traffic to the new revision until all users have exercised it because rollback would hide the defect.
Change the route table without checking target health or invoice data because network rollback reverses application writes.

feedback.Reason: Rollback should restore serving behavior while preserving the failed artifact and handling side effects already produced by the bad revision.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Immutable revisions and controlled traffic shifting allow rapid reversal. Business writes are not automatically undone by deployment rollback and require reconciliation or compensation.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team shifts traffic back, freezes or isolates bad writes, compares invoice outcomes, and records the defect before a corrected rollout.
Details.errorCorrection: Deleting evidence prevents diagnosis, continuing traffic expands impact, and network changes do not reverse committed business writes.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Rollback may leave mixed-version data or schema state; backward-compatible contracts and explicit data repair are part of deployment design.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: The failed artifact and logs are needed for diagnosis and audit.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Continuing traffic expands customer impact after a confirmed correctness failure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Traffic rollback cannot undo application-side invoice writes automatically.

items.prompt: A company needs a cloud API tier, an on-premises adapter for a factory protocol, and a low-latency local analytics worker. Which placement decision is coherent?
constraints: The API can run in an AWS Region.
The factory protocol is reachable only on premises.
Local analytics has a latency and data-residency requirement.

options.text: Place each workload in a capacity model that satisfies its boundary—Regional ECS or EKS for the API, ECS Anywhere or suitable on-premises capacity for the adapter, and Outposts or local capacity for analytics—then define private connectivity and ownership.
Run every workload in the Region because one centralized placement always minimizes operational risk regardless of latency and protocol constraints.
Run every workload on premises because cloud services cannot participate in a hybrid container architecture.
Choose placement from container image size alone because location does not affect dependencies.

feedback.Reason: Hybrid placement should follow workload latency, connectivity, residency, and operating constraints rather than force one location onto every component.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: ECS, EKS, ECS Anywhere, Outposts, and other capacity options expose different control, locality, and operational boundaries. The application contract must include cross-location connectivity and failure behavior.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect keeps public API traffic in the Region, places protocol-dependent work near the factory, and tests data flow when Regional or site connectivity is degraded.
Details.errorCorrection: A single Region can violate hard local constraints, cloud services can manage hybrid workloads, and image size does not determine placement.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Every additional location adds deployment, observability, data movement, and failure complexity; only hard requirements should justify it.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Centralization can violate local latency, protocol, or residency constraints.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: AWS provides supported hybrid container management and connectivity patterns.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Image size is one deployment property and does not describe latency, data, or network dependencies.
